article.headline: Bitcoin's Longevity Quietly Undermines the Tulip-Bubble Analogy
article.lede: Among the stock retorts to Bitcoin enthusiasm, the tulip comparison is the most durable — and, its critics increasingly argue, the least accurate. A clip of British financial writer Dominic Frisby laying out this counter-argument has circulated widely among Bitcoin advocates, amplified here by @noahkaufmanmd as a ready rebuttal for skeptics.
article.body:
The *tulip mania* of 1637 — in which Dutch speculators drove prices for rare bulb varieties to extraordinary heights before the market collapsed almost overnight — has served as shorthand for irrational exuberance for nearly four centuries. The episode lasted roughly three years from speculative peak to ruin. It is, structurally, a puncture story: a thing inflated, then gone, with no second act.

**Bitcoin** presents a structurally different pattern. Launched in 2009, it has now survived fifteen years and several dramatic price cycles, losing eighty percent or more of its value on multiple occasions, only to recover and establish new highs. Frisby's point is essentially definitional: *speculative bubbles*, by their nature, do not recover. What deflates to zero in 1637 and never returns fits the definition. What cycles through boom and bust across a decade and a half — retaining and growing a user base, attracting institutional capital, and prompting sovereign nations to adopt it as legal tender — does not fit it as cleanly.

The longevity argument is not a proof that Bitcoin has intrinsic value; that remains a separate and genuinely contested question. A tulip bulb had no lasting utility beyond ornament, while Bitcoin's proponents point to its fixed supply cap of 21 million units, its role as a *decentralized* settlement network, and its growing acceptance as an institutional-grade *store of value*. Whether those properties justify its price at any given moment is exactly the debate the tulip analogy is meant to foreclose — and the counter-argument is essentially a plea to keep the question open rather than dismiss it with a seventeenth-century reference.

Frisby, whose 2014 book *Bitcoin: The Future of Money?* was among the earliest serious popular treatments of the asset, has long been one of its more articulate advocates. The clip does not appear to make a full valuation case; its contribution is narrower and more rhetorical — clearing away a piece of faulty analogy so that the substantive argument can actually begin.

concepts.definition: A speculative episode in the Dutch Republic during 1634–1637 in which prices for certain tulip bulb varieties rose to extreme levels before collapsing abruptly in February 1637. It is widely cited as the first recorded speculative bubble, though historians debate how broad or devastating the crash actually was beyond a small circle of professional traders.

A market condition in which asset prices rise well above any plausible intrinsic value, sustained by the expectation that prices will keep rising and that each buyer can find a later buyer willing to pay more. Bubbles are typically identified in retrospect and resolve through a rapid collapse rather than a gradual decline.

An asset that reliably preserves purchasing power over time. Gold is the canonical example. Bitcoin proponents argue it qualifies because its supply is algorithmically capped at 21 million units, making it resistant to inflationary dilution — though critics note its price volatility undermines this claim in practice.

A system with no single controlling authority. Bitcoin transactions are verified by a distributed global network of computers (miners) rather than a bank or government, meaning no single actor can unilaterally alter the ledger or freeze funds.

Bitcoin's protocol limits the total number of coins that will ever exist to 21 million. This hard ceiling, written into the code and enforced by network consensus, is central to the store-of-value argument: unlike fiat currencies, no central bank can expand the supply.

books.title: Bitcoin: The Future of Money?
books.author: Dominic Frisby
books.summary: Published in 2014, this was among the first mainstream books to treat Bitcoin as a serious monetary innovation rather than a curiosity. Frisby, a British comedian and financial writer, traces the history of money and argues that Bitcoin's fixed supply and decentralized architecture position it as a credible alternative to state-issued currency. It remains a readable entry point for readers approaching the subject without a technical background.

sources.title: Tulip Mania vs the Cryptocurrency of Today
sources.note: Provides the 1634–1637 dates for tulip mania and contrasts the speculative mechanics with Bitcoin's blockchain utility argument

sources.title: Tulip Mania: The First Financial Bubble and Its Comparison to Bitcoin
sources.note: Secondary comparison source confirming the rapid collapse timeline of the tulip episode

poster_noahkaufmanmd.bio_summary: Board-certified emergency physician, financial educator, and Bitcoin advocate. Co-founder of the Crypto Pulse newsletter, author of 'Self Bitcoinization', and a recurring podcast guest on physician finance and digital assets. Posts at the intersection of personal finance, monetary theory, and Bitcoin — arguing that understanding Bitcoin is a professional obligation for physicians managing their own financial futures. Tone is earnest, educational, and unapologetically pro-Bitcoin.

notable_works.title: Self Bitcoinization
notable_works.note: A philosophy-of-Bitcoin book exploring the case for individuals adopting a Bitcoin-centric financial posture.

affiliation_history.note: Bi-weekly educational newsletter on crypto investing, aimed at healthcare professionals.
